items.prompt: How does a dolphin sleep without drowning?

options.label: Half its brain sleeps at a time
options.feedback: The other half keeps it swimming and surfacing.

options.label: It floats motionless at the surface
options.feedback: It must keep moving to hold position and breathe.

options.label: It holds its breath and sinks
options.feedback: It would drown before waking.

options.label: It does not sleep at all
options.feedback: It sleeps, but not the way we do.

items.ok_line: One hemisphere off, one on, with the matching eye shut.
items.ko_line: A dolphin must choose to breathe. What does that rule out?
items.exp_title: Sleeping with one eye open, literally
items.exp_text: A dolphin's breathing is voluntary — it must decide to surface — so it cannot afford to switch off completely. It sleeps one hemisphere at a time for a couple of hours, closing the opposite eye, then swaps. Some birds do the same on long migrations, and ducks at the edge of a sleeping group keep the outward-facing eye open while those in the middle sleep with both shut.

items.prompt: How does a swift sleep during months in the air?

options.label: It sleeps while gliding at height
options.feedback: It climbs at dusk and dozes on the way down.

options.label: It lands briefly each night
options.feedback: Tracked swifts stay aloft for ten months.

options.label: It sleeps on the water
options.feedback: A swift cannot take off from water.

options.label: It goes without sleep entirely
options.feedback: No animal manages that for months.

items.ok_line: It climbs at dusk and sleeps on the long way down.
items.ko_line: A swift can go ten months without touching anything. Where else could it sleep?
items.exp_text: Tracking devices showed common swifts staying airborne for up to ten months without once coming down — they feed, drink and mate on the wing. At dusk they climb to two or three kilometres and descend slowly through the night, apparently sleeping one hemisphere at a time. A swift that hatched this summer may not touch anything solid until it first nests, two years later.

items.prompt: Why can a horse sleep standing up?

options.label: Its legs lock in place
options.feedback: Tendons hold the joints without muscle effort.

options.label: It never truly falls asleep
options.feedback: It does sleep, and deeply at times.

options.label: It leans against something solid
options.feedback: A horse in an open field manages alone.

options.label: Its hooves grip the ground
options.feedback: Grip does not keep a body upright.

items.ok_line: The joints lock, and no muscle has to hold anything.
items.ko_line: Standing normally costs constant effort. What if it did not have to?
items.exp_text: A horse has a stay apparatus, an arrangement of tendons and ligaments that locks the leg joints so it can rest without muscular effort. It matters because a horse is prey: getting up takes precious seconds. But locking only allows light sleep — for deep sleep with full muscle relaxation it must lie down, which it does for less than an hour a day, often while another horse stands watch.

options.label: Body functions slowed to survive winter
options.feedback: Temperature, heartbeat and breathing all drop steeply.

options.label: A long ordinary sleep
options.feedback: Hibernation is physiologically quite different from sleep.

options.label: Staying still to avoid predators
options.feedback: Hiding is a separate behaviour.

options.label: Living off stored food underground
options.feedback: Some store food, but that is not hibernation.

items.ok_line: Not deep sleep — the whole body turned down.
items.ko_line: A hibernating animal's heart may beat a few times a minute. Is that sleep?
items.exp_title: The body turned down, not switched off
items.exp_text: A hibernating ground squirrel drops to near freezing, its heart slowing from 200 beats a minute to about five and its breathing to a few times an hour. It is not sleep: brain activity looks quite different, and the animal must periodically warm up and sleep properly, which is one of the costliest parts of the whole winter. Rousing takes hours and burns a large share of the stored fat.

options.label: It enters a lighter state called torpor
options.feedback: Its temperature drops only a few degrees.

options.label: Yes, exactly like a ground squirrel
options.feedback: A squirrel drops close to freezing; a bear does not.

options.label: No, it stays fully active all winter
options.feedback: It does den up and slow down markedly.

options.label: It sleeps normally, just for longer
options.feedback: Its whole metabolism changes, which sleep does not.

items.ok_line: Deeply drowsy rather than deeply cold — and it can wake at once.
items.ko_line: A bear can be roused within seconds. A true hibernator takes hours.
items.exp_text: A bear's temperature falls only about five degrees and its heart slows to perhaps ten beats a minute, but it can rouse fully within seconds — which is why den disturbance is dangerous. It goes months without eating, drinking or passing waste, recycling its own urea into protein, and females give birth and nurse cubs mid-winter without waking properly. It loses fat but barely any muscle, an ability medicine would very much like to understand.

items.prompt: How long does a giraffe sleep each day?

options.label: Around half an hour
options.feedback: In short bursts of a few minutes at a time.

options.label: Around eight hours
options.feedback: That is a human's share, not a giraffe's.

options.label: Around fifteen hours
options.feedback: That belongs to cats and some bats.

options.label: It does not sleep at all
options.feedback: Every animal studied sleeps in some form.

items.ok_line: About thirty minutes a day, taken a few minutes at a time.
items.ko_line: It is prey, it is enormous, and getting up takes a long time. Guess low.
items.exp_title: The lightest sleeper on the savannah
items.exp_text: Giraffes sleep around thirty minutes in twenty-four hours, mostly standing, in bursts of a few minutes. Deep sleep requires lying with the head curled back onto the rump, and they risk that for only a few minutes at a time — standing up again takes long enough to be fatal with lions about. Grazing animals generally sleep least; predators, who fear nothing, sleep most.

items.prompt: Why do bats hang upside down to rest?

options.label: Their feet grip without effort
options.feedback: The tendons lock under the body's own weight.

options.label: It keeps blood in the head
options.feedback: Circulation is not the reason.

options.label: It hides them from below
options.feedback: Hanging in the open makes them very visible.

options.label: They cannot turn the right way up
options.feedback: They can turn easily; they choose not to.

items.ok_line: Weight does the gripping. Letting go takes the effort.
items.ko_line: A sleeping bat does not fall. Ask what is holding it, and what that costs.
items.exp_text: A bat's toe tendons run so that the weight of the hanging body pulls the claws closed — it grips without using any muscle, and a dead bat stays hanging. It also solves a launch problem: a bat's wings cannot generate enough lift from a standing start, so hanging high means it need only let go and fall into flight.

items.prompt: How does a sea otter avoid drifting away while it sleeps?

options.label: It wraps itself in kelp
options.feedback: Or holds another otter's paw.

options.label: It sleeps on the seabed
options.feedback: It would drown before waking.

options.label: It swims slowly in its sleep
options.feedback: Otters sleep floating and still.

options.label: It comes ashore every night
options.feedback: Sea otters can spend their whole lives at sea.

items.ok_line: Anchored in seaweed, or holding on to a neighbour.
items.ko_line: It floats on its back all night. What might stop it drifting?
items.exp_title: Anchored in kelp, or in company
items.exp_text: Sea otters sleep floating on their backs and wrap themselves in strands of kelp to stay put in the current. Where there is no kelp they hold paws with one another, drifting as a raft — groups of a hundred or more have been recorded. They also keep their forepaws raised out of the water, since those paws lose heat fastest and an otter has no blubber to spare.

items.prompt: What is unusual about the way birds sleep during migration?

options.label: They sleep in bursts of seconds
options.feedback: Hundreds of brief naps, often mid-flight.

options.label: They stop sleeping for weeks
options.feedback: Sleep is reduced, never abandoned.

options.label: They sleep more than usual
options.feedback: Migration cuts sleep sharply.

options.label: They sleep only after landing
options.feedback: Some routes offer nowhere to land at all.

items.ok_line: Naps measured in seconds, taken hundreds of times a day.
items.ko_line: The bird cannot stop and cannot go without sleep. What is left?
items.exp_text: Frigatebirds fitted with brain recorders were found sleeping in flight for about forty minutes a day, in bursts of a few seconds, often with one hemisphere at a time and usually while circling upward on rising air. On land the same birds sleep more than twelve hours. Migrating songbirds take hundreds of naps of a few seconds each, and perform normally on a fraction of their usual rest.

items.prompt: Why do nocturnal animals sleep through the day?

options.label: Their body clock is set that way
options.feedback: An internal rhythm keeps running even without daylight.

options.label: Daylight physically hurts them
options.feedback: Most tolerate daylight perfectly well.

options.label: They are simply tired by morning
options.feedback: Tiredness would not hold the pattern so precisely.

options.label: Their food is only out at night
options.feedback: Often true, but the clock runs regardless.

items.ok_line: An internal clock, running whether or not the Sun cooperates.
items.ko_line: Kept in constant darkness, the animal keeps almost the same schedule. What does that show?
items.exp_title: A clock that runs without the Sun
items.exp_text: Almost every living thing carries an internal cycle of roughly twenty-four hours, driven by proteins that build up and break down at a steady rate. Kept in constant darkness, animals keep near-normal schedules for weeks, drifting only slowly — which shows the rhythm is generated internally and merely corrected by daylight. The same clock governs your own alertness, temperature and appetite, and jet lag is it running out of step.
